ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: Ethical approval was obtained from the VU Scientific and Ethical Review Board (reference number 2020.088) and the trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID NCT05582954).
Participants were not offered any compensation for filling out questionnaires.

The present study utilized the following inclusion criteria: participants had to 1) be aged 16 years or older, 2) be currently enrolled as a student or PhD candidate at a university within the Caring University Consortium, and 3) provide informed consent.
Upon completion of the program, participants were awarded a certificate of completion.
Upon meeting milestone achievements such as completing a module or filling out the post-measure, participants were rewarded a colorful digital 'badge'.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the regular or gamified condition using 1:1 block randomization via an automated system embedded within the Caring Universities platform.
All randomized participants were included in the primary analyses following the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle.

As an additional sensitivity analysis, we compared adherence rates between the two arms for participants who completed at least 1 module, as these participants are guaranteed to have been exposed to the gamification elements.Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were calculated manually, using the benchmarks of .2, .5, and .8 as small, moderate, and large effects respectively (Cohen, 2013).
table.formatted: As an additional sensitivity analysis, we compared adherence rates between the two arms for participants who completed at least 1 module, as these participants are guaranteed to have been exposed to the gamification elements.Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were calculated manually, using the benchmarks of .2, .5, and .8 as small, moderate, and large effects respectively <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Cohen, 2013)</ref>.

table.text: A total of 1,026 participants were assessed for eligibility between November 2022 and October 2025.
A total of 873 participants completed the baseline assessment, were randomized and were offered access to the intervention, making up the total sample.

Most participants were born in the Netherlands (62.1%) or another European country (28.2%), and were primarily enrolled in their first year of a bachelor's program (25.2%) or a master's program (37.7%).

As an additional sensitivity analysis, we compared the adherence between the two arms for intervention starters, as these participants are guaranteed to have been exposed to the gamification elements.

The analyses revealed that participants completed significantly more modules in the gamified intervention (n = 280, M = 2.86, SD = 1.25) than in the non-gamified intervention (n = 282, M = 2.64, SD = 1.28), t(560) = 2.051, p = .041, with a small effect size (Cohen's d = .17).

power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: We could find no prior literature comparing gamified and non-gamified digital mental health interventions to inform the sample size estimation. Therefore we conducted a power calculation for a two-tailed difference between means with a small-tomoderate effect size of .3 (Cohen, 2013), which is still clinically meaningful. This indicated a total required sample size of n=580 (290 per study arm with complete data) (Faul et al., 2007).

summary_table.ethics_statements: Ethical approval was obtained from the VU Scientific and Ethical Review Board (reference number 2020.088) and the trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID NCT05582954).
live_data_statements: Participants were not offered any compensation for filling out questionnaires.

The present study utilized the following inclusion criteria: participants had to 1) be aged 16 years or older, 2) be currently enrolled as a student or PhD candidate at a university within the Caring University Consortium, and 3) provide informed consent.
Upon completion of the program, participants were awarded a certificate of completion.
Upon meeting milestone achievements such as completing a module or filling out the post-measure, participants were rewarded a colorful digital 'badge'.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the regular or gamified condition using 1:1 block randomization via an automated system embedded within the Caring Universities platform.
All randomized participants were included in the primary analyses following the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle.

As an additional sensitivity analysis, we compared adherence rates between the two arms for participants who completed at least 1 module, as these participants are guaranteed to have been exposed to the gamification elements.Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were calculated manually, using the benchmarks of .2, .5, and .8 as small, moderate, and large effects respectively (Cohen, 2013).
A total of 1,026 participants were assessed for eligibility between November 2022 and October 2025.
A total of 873 participants completed the baseline assessment, were randomized and were offered access to the intervention, making up the total sample.

Most participants were born in the Netherlands (62.1%) or another European country (28.2%), and were primarily enrolled in their first year of a bachelor's program (25.2%) or a master's program (37.7%).

As an additional sensitivity analysis, we compared the adherence between the two arms for intervention starters, as these participants are guaranteed to have been exposed to the gamification elements.

The analyses revealed that participants completed significantly more modules in the gamified intervention (n = 280, M = 2.86, SD = 1.25) than in the non-gamified intervention (n = 282, M = 2.64, SD = 1.28), t(560) = 2.051, p = .041, with a small effect size (Cohen's d = .17).

text.text: Background: Mental health problems and low self-esteem are highly prevalent among college students and are associated with impaired academic functioning and poorer long-term well-being.
Digital interventions are a promising and scalable approach to improve student mental health, but adherence is often limited.
Gamification may improve engagement, though evidence remains scarce.
Objective: This study examines whether adding gamification elements to a guided digital CBT-based self-esteem intervention for students improves adherence, satisfaction, and mental health outcomes.
Methods: In a randomized controlled trial, 873 students were allocated to a gamified or non-gamified version of a guided self-esteem intervention.
The primary outcome was adherence (number of modules completed), while secondary outcomes included satisfaction, self-esteem, depressive symptoms, anxiety, and quality of life.
Assessments were conducted at baseline and at 4-week follow-up.
Results: No significant differences were found between conditions on adherence, satisfaction or clinical outcomes in the full sample.
Among intervention starters (i.e. completed ≥1 module), the gamified version showed a small increase in adherence (d = .17).
Across conditions, participants showed significant improvements in selfesteem, depression, anxiety, and quality of life from pre-to post-test (d = .44-.76).
Conclusions: Gamification may modestly increase adherence among intervention starters but does not improve satisfaction or clinical outcomes.
Both intervention versions were associated with improvements over time; however, the lack of an untreated control condition limits causal interpretation.
Future research should investigate mechanisms behind gamification components.

text.text: Meta-analytic evidence indicates that psychological treatments can effectively address low self-esteem in adults, with CBT emerging as particularly effective (Kolubinski et al., 2018; Niveau et al., 2021).

text.text: Despite their effectiveness, access to such interventions is often limited by stigma, preference for self-reliance, and practical constraints such as cost, time, and geography (Russell et al., 2008; Vidourek et al., 2014).

text.text: Digital interventions may help address these barriers due to their accessibility, anonymity, and scalability (Andersson & Titov, 2014; Ebert et al., 2017; Liu et al., 2023).

text.text: While empirical evidence on digital self-esteem interventions for college students remains scarce, they show promising effects.

One unguided mobile self-esteem intervention demonstrated small-to-moderate effects (Bruhns et al., 2021), and a therapist-supported CBT-based online intervention showed large effects (Berg et al., 2022).

text.text: Although encouraging, these studies differ substantially in format (i.e. mobile versus web-based), adherence operationalization and level of guidance, limiting conclusions about usage and scalability.
Moreover, therapist-guided interventions may be difficult to scale due to limited mental health workforce capacity (Ballout, 2025).
text.formatted: Moreover, therapist-guided interventions may be difficult to scale due to limited mental health workforce capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Ballout, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Despite the advantages of digital mental health interventions, one often-reported challenge is low adherence, which is the extent to which participants follow the therapy as prescribed (Religioni et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Despite the advantages of digital mental health interventions, one often-reported challenge is low adherence, which is the extent to which participants follow the therapy as prescribed <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Religioni et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Dropout rates in digital interventions are generally high, often exceeding 50% in real-world settings (Kelders et al., 2012; Nwosu et al., 2022), and are particularly elevated in unguided formats (Karyotaki et al., 2021; Opie et al., 2024).

text.text: In digital mental health interventions, greater adherence is often associated with better treatment outcomes (Donkin et al., 2011).

text.text: Low adherence rates may compromise the effectiveness of digital interventions and diminish their potential to produce significant health outcomes (Linardon & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, 2020).

text.text: One possible approach to increase adherence in digital interventions is through gamification, which refers to the application of game design elements in non-game contexts to enhance engagement and promote desired mental health benefits (Castellano-Tejedor & Cencerrado, 2024; Deterding et al., 2011).

text.text: Rather than transforming an intervention into a literal game, gamification entails integrating features from (digital) games into digital interventions.

For example, participants may receive visual feedback on their progress, unlock bonus materials as a reward, or earn badges and certificates upon reaching milestones. (Aschentrup et al., 2024; Tondello et al., 2017).

text.text: These elements may increase adherence through several psychological mechanisms, such as reinforcing behavioral change, stimulating curiosity and interest (V. W. S. Cheng et al., 2019), and nurturing intrinsic motivation and sustaining engagement over time (Ryan et al., 2006; Seaborn & Fels, 2015).

text.text: A growing body of research indicates the potential of gamification in digital interventions.

One systematic review found that gamified interventions increased engagement (e.g. time spent, interaction with the intervention, visits) among adults compared to interventions without gamification (Looyestyn et al., 2017).
text.formatted: One systematic review found that gamified interventions increased engagement (e.g. time spent, interaction with the intervention, visits) among adults compared to interventions without gamification <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Looyestyn et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Another systematic review suggests there may be a relationship between number of gamification elements and adherence: as one increases, so may the other (Brown et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Another systematic review suggests there may be a relationship between number of gamification elements and adherence: as one increases, so may the other <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Brown et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond engagement, meta-analytic evidence suggests that gamified interventions may contribute to mental health outcomes, including improved general well-being, anxiety, and depression (C. Cheng & Ebrahimi, 2023).
text.formatted: Beyond engagement, meta-analytic evidence suggests that gamified interventions may contribute to mental health outcomes, including improved general well-being, anxiety, and depression (C. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cheng & Ebrahimi, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence in student populations specifically shows similar trends.
One randomized controlled trial (RCT) found that a gamified mental health app had higher retention than a different, non-gamified app (Litvin et al., 2023).
text.formatted: One randomized controlled trial (RCT) found that a gamified mental health app had higher retention than a different, non-gamified app <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">(Litvin et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In another RCT, a gamified intervention performed comparably to a group CBT intervention, with both interventions resulting in greater reductions in anxiety and depression than a moodmonitoring control condition (Bantjes et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In another RCT, a gamified intervention performed comparably to a group CBT intervention, with both interventions resulting in greater reductions in anxiety and depression than a moodmonitoring control condition <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bantjes et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A gamified CBT intervention showed promising effects in reducing dysfunctional negative emotions and irrational cognition among college students (Tomoiagă & David, 2022).
text.formatted: A gamified CBT intervention showed promising effects in reducing dysfunctional negative emotions and irrational cognition among college students <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">(Tomoiagă & David, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Combined, these studies suggest that college students may benefit from gamified digital interventions in terms of both engagement and effectiveness.
However, the evidence on gamification of mental health interventions for the student population remains scarce and several important gaps persist.
To our knowledge, no study has isolated and examined the effect of gamification on treatment adherence and effectiveness.

Additionally, though low self-esteem poses a crucial developmental challenge for college students and is associated with a range of negative mental health outcomes, we found no trials on gamification within interventions targeting low self-esteem in this population.
For the present study, we developed a guided CBT-based digital intervention for low self-esteem tailored to college students in the Netherlands (EsteemUp).
We conducted an RCT comparing two versions of the intervention: one with gamification elements and one without.
The primary aim was to examine whether gamification improves adherence, operationalized as the number of completed modules.

In addition, we examined whether gamification positively impacted participants' satisfaction, changes in self-esteem, depression, anxiety, and quality of life, as well as the relationship between adherence and clinical outcomes.
We hypothesized that participants in the gamified condition would show greater adherence and more favorable outcomes than participants in the non-gamified condition.
>Methods

text.text: This study is a two-arm randomized trial comparing the effectiveness of two versions of a guided e-health intervention, EsteemUp, in enhancing students' self-esteem: a standard (non-gamified) version and a gamified version.
Assessments were conducted at baseline (T0) and at post-intervention four weeks later (T1).

This study was conducted within the Caring Universities Consortium; a collaboration between -at the time of the trial --seven Dutch universities (VU Amsterdam, Leiden University, Maastricht University, Utrecht University, Erasmus University, University of Amsterdam and Inholland University of Applied Sciences).
The Caring Universities Consortium is affiliated with the World Health Organization (WHO) World Mental Health International College Student Initiative (WMH-ICS) (Cuijpers et al., 2019).
text.formatted: The Caring Universities Consortium is affiliated with the World Health Organization (WHO) World Mental Health International College Student Initiative (WMH-ICS) <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Cuijpers et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Ethical approval was obtained from the VU Scientific and Ethical Review Board (reference number 2020.088) and the trial was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (ID NCT05582954).
Participants in this study were undergraduate, graduate, or PhD students in the Netherlands.
Eligible students could register for the EsteemUp program through multiple recruitment channels.
First, through the annual WMH-ICS survey on student mental health, which is sent via email to all enrolled students.
Second, Caring Universities conducted both online (e.g., social media) and offline (e.g., posters, flyers) marketing efforts to recruit participants.
Finally, university staff members who work directly with students (e.g. student psychologists, study advisors, mentors, lecturers) were encouraged to refer students to the program.
Participant recruitment and data collection took place from November 2022 to October 2025.
Participants were not offered any compensation for filling out questionnaires.

The present study utilized the following inclusion criteria: participants had to 1) be aged 16 years or older, 2) be currently enrolled as a student or PhD candidate at a university within the Caring University Consortium, and 3) provide informed consent.
There was no inclusion criterion with respect so selfesteem.
EsteemUp is an online intervention designed to improve students' self-esteem.
It was developed based on evidence-based psychological techniques and treatments (i.e.
CBT) and shaped by student input to better align the intervention with their needs and preferences.

EsteemUp consists of 4 modules incorporating multiple evidence-based therapeutic components, primarily grounded in Cognitive Behavioral Therapy (CBT), complemented by elements from positive psychology and social skills training.
Intervention content can be found in Table 1.
text.formatted: Intervention content can be found in Table <ref type="table">1</ref>.

text.text: Each module took approximately 30 to 45 minutes to complete and included a combination of psychoeducation, reflective questions, interactive exercises, and homework assignments.
The contents were presented through a mix of text and visual media (e.g. illustrations, infographics, videos) to enhance engagement.
While students were encouraged to complete one module per week, they were free to proceed at their own pace.
The program was accessible via any internet-connected device.

The gamified version of EsteemUp incorporated several core gamification elements designed to enhance user engagement and motivation (Hamari, 2017; Hervas et al., 2017; Mazarakis & Bräuer, 2023).

text.text: The elements were selected on the basis of technical feasibility from a larger set of gamification elements that have been shown in a systematic review to have positive effects on motivation and engagement-related psychological outcomes or behavior-related outcomes (Hamari et al., 2014).

text.text: The homepage included a visual progress bar that showed participants how much of the program (i.e. how many of the four modules) they had completed.
It included short motivational messages such as 'Halfway there!' after completing two modules or 'Only one to go!' upon completing three modules.

Upon completion of the program, participants were awarded a certificate of completion.
This certificate acted as a form of symbolic validation and recognition of the time and effort they put into completing the program.
See Figure 2.

text.text: Upon meeting milestone achievements such as completing a module or filling out the post-measure, participants were rewarded a colorful digital 'badge'.
The intervention also included one page containing all badges, in which badges that were not yet obtained were teased with the symbol of a grey question mark.

Finally, upon completion of each module, participants could download an aesthetically pleasing handout containing a summary of the module.
These handouts were framed as bonus content one would unlock by doing more of the program.

text.text: Participants in both conditions were supported by a student e-coach.
E-coaches were third year bachelor or (research) master students in Clinical Psychology at Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam.
E-coaches provided asynchronous, text-based feedback via the platform after each module completed by a participant.
This feedback was personalized based on the participant's answers to reflective questions and assignments.

The goal was to increase motivation and engagement by showing empathy, offering affirmations, asking open-ended questions, and using reflective techniques, which is in line with motivational interviewing principles (Hall et al., 2012).
text.formatted: The goal was to increase motivation and engagement by showing empathy, offering affirmations, asking open-ended questions, and using reflective techniques, which is in line with motivational interviewing principles <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hall et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: E-coaches received six hours of training as preparation and were required to attend weekly intervision sessions supervised by the research team.
As additional quality assurance, the e-coaching messages were periodically examined on a sample basis by the research team.
Participants were randomly assigned to either the regular or gamified condition using 1:1 block randomization via an automated system embedded within the Caring Universities platform.
Randomization was stratified by gender and university, and conditions were allocated automatically upon completion of the baseline assessment.
This automated process ensured allocation concealment and blinding.

The following sociodemographic information was obtained: age, gender, marital status, nationality, current university, faculty, education level (Bachelor, Master or PhD.), and current usage of psychotherapy (yes/no) and/or psychotropic medication (yes/no).
Adherence was operationalized as the number of modules completed by each participant, with a total of four modules available in the intervention.
General participant satisfaction with the intervention was assessed using the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8) (Larsen et al., 1979).
text.formatted: General participant satisfaction with the intervention was assessed using the Client Satisfaction Questionnaire (CSQ-8) <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">(Larsen et al., 1979)</ref>.

text.text: The CSQ-8 consists of eight items rated on a 4-point Likert scale, yielding a total score ranging from 8 to 32, with higher scores indicating greater satisfaction.

Example items include 'In an overall, general sense, how satisfied are you with the service you have received?' and 'If a friend were in need of similar help, would you recommend our program to him or her?'.
Though there are no formally established cut-off scores for different levels of satisfaction, previous research has proposed interpretative ranges.

One article classified scores of 8-20 as low satisfaction, 21-26 as moderate satisfaction, and 27-32 as high satisfaction (Jilani et al., 2023), whereas another suggested that scores between 24 and 32 reflect high levels of satisfaction (Ozmen et al., 2023).
text.formatted: One article classified scores of 8-20 as low satisfaction, 21-26 as moderate satisfaction, and 27-32 as high satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Jilani et al., 2023)</ref>, whereas another suggested that scores between 24 and 32 reflect high levels of satisfaction <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">(Ozmen et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The instrument has demonstrated good model fit, high internal consistency, and strong construct validity in the context of online interventions (Boß et al., 2016).
text.formatted: The instrument has demonstrated good model fit, high internal consistency, and strong construct validity in the context of online interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Boß et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The Dutch adaptation demonstrated similar psychometric properties and was considered appropriate for use in the Netherlands. (de Brey, 1983; De Wilde & Hendriks, 2005).

text.text: Satisfaction with the e-coach was measured using the Working Alliance Inventory for guided internet interventions (WAI-I) (Gómez Penedo et al., 2020).

The WAI-I consists of 12 items rated on a 5-point Likert scale, producing a total score ranging from 12 to 60 with higher scores indicating a stronger working alliance and greater satisfaction with the e-coach.
Example items include 'I believe the e-coach who supports me in the online program likes me' and 'The e-coach who supports me in the online program is really interested in my well-being'.
Scores between 36 and 47 reflect sufficient satisfaction, while scores above 48 indicate high to very high satisfaction.
The WAI-I has demonstrated adequate psychometric properties, including good reliability and validity in the context of guided internet-based interventions (Gómez Penedo et al., 2020).
Self-esteem was assessed using the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) (Rosenberg, 1965), one of the most widely used instruments for measuring global self-esteem.
text.formatted: Self-esteem was assessed using the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSES) <ref type="bibr" target="#b71">(Rosenberg, 1965)</ref>, one of the most widely used instruments for measuring global self-esteem.

text.text: The RSES consists of 10 items rated on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 4 (strongly agree), with higher scores indicating higher self-esteem.
Five items are positively worded (e.g., "On the whole, I am satisfied with myself") and five are negatively worded and reverse-scored (e.g., "At times I think I am no good at all.").
The scale has demonstrated strong psychometric properties, including good internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and construct validity (Sinclair et al., 2010).
text.formatted: The scale has demonstrated strong psychometric properties, including good internal consistency, test-retest reliability, and construct validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Sinclair et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) (Kroenke et al., 2001), a widely used self-report measure of depression severity.
text.formatted: Depressive symptoms were assessed using the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Kroenke et al., 2001)</ref>, a widely used self-report measure of depression severity.

text.text: The PHQ-9 consists of nine items rated on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 0 ("not at all") to 3 ("nearly every day"), yielding a total score between 0 and 27, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.
The instrument has demonstrated strong psychometric properties, including high sensitivity, specificity, test-retest reliability, and construct validity (Kroenke et al., 2001; Wittkampf et al., 2007)

text.text: Anxiety symptoms were measured using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7) (Spitzer et al., 2006), a brief self-report instrument designed to assess the severity of generalized anxiety symptoms.
text.formatted: Anxiety symptoms were measured using the Generalized Anxiety Disorder 7-item scale (GAD-7) <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">(Spitzer et al., 2006)</ref>, a brief self-report instrument designed to assess the severity of generalized anxiety symptoms.

text.text: Each of the seven items is rated on a 4-point Likert scale ranging from 0 ("not at all") to 3 ("nearly every day"), resulting in a total score between 0 and 21, with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity.

The GAD-7 has demonstrated strong psychometric properties, including high internal consistency, sensitivity, specificity, test-retest reliability, and construct validity (Löwe et al., 2008; Rutter & Brown, 2017; Spitzer et al., 2006).

text.text: Quality of life was assessed using the Mental Health Quality of Life questionnaire (MHQoL) (van Krugten et al., 2022), a brief instrument specifically developed to measure quality of life in individuals with mental health problems.

text.text: Statistical analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS version 30 and Stata version 18.
All randomized participants were included in the primary analyses following the intention-to-treat (ITT) principle.

To verify the success of the randomization, baseline differences between the two study arms ('regular' vs. 'gamified' condition) were examined using Chi-square tests for categorical variables and independent samples t-tests for continuous variables.
The same tests were applied to assess potential differences between study completers and non-completers.
Adherence rates were compared between study arms for the total sample using an independent samples t-test.

As an additional sensitivity analysis, we compared adherence rates between the two arms for participants who completed at least 1 module, as these participants are guaranteed to have been exposed to the gamification elements.Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were calculated manually, using the benchmarks of .2, .5, and .8 as small, moderate, and large effects respectively (Cohen, 2013).

text.text: As an exploratory analysis, we examined the association between adherence and post-intervention clinical outcomes using multiple linear regression models, controlling for baseline clinical scores.
Adherence was evaluated as a predictor in the full sample and separately within each intervention arm.
Missing outcome data were addressed using multiple imputation, with 70 datasets generated through Fully Conditional Specification (FCS).
Parameter estimates were pooled according to Rubin's rules.
Group differences in satisfaction (CSQ-8, WAI-I) were analyzed using independent samples t-tests on the imputed data.
We explored changes in clinical outcomes of self-esteem (RSES), depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and quality of life (MHQoL) with linear mixed-effects models (LMMs).

The LMMs were conducted using the unimputed dataset, given prior evidence that LMMs applied to longitudinal data can appropriately address missingness without the need for multiple imputation (Twisk et al., 2013).

text.text: As covariates we included baseline clinical severity, age, gender, marital status, nationality, university affiliation, educational level, and current psychotherapy and/or medication use (Ebert et al., 2013; Karyotaki et al., 2018; Reins et al., 2020).

Effect sizes (Cohen's d) were calculated manually based on the EMMs.
As additional sensitivity analyses, we repeated all analyses for participants who had completed at least one module and were therefore guaranteed to have been exposed to the gamification elements.
>Results

text.text: A total of 1,026 participants were assessed for eligibility between November 2022 and October 2025.
Of these, 153 dropped out during baseline assessment or account creation and were not randomized.
A total of 873 participants completed the baseline assessment, were randomized and were offered access to the intervention, making up the total sample.
Of these, 434 were allocated to the gamified intervention and 439 to the non-gamified intervention.
In the gamified intervention, 280 started the intervention by completing at least one module ("intervention starters"), and 282 did in the non-gamified intervention.
See Figure 5 for the participant flowchart.

text.text: The mean age of the total sample (n = 873) was 22.99 years (SD = 4.49), and most participants identified as female (79.5%).

Most participants were born in the Netherlands (62.1%) or another European country (28.2%), and were primarily enrolled in their first year of a bachelor's program (25.2%) or a master's program (37.7%).
A majority was single (60%) and not currently receiving psychotherapy or medication (79.4%).

On average, participants displayed moderate self-esteem (i.e. neither particularly low nor high self-evaluation) and quality of life (RSES M =23.64; MHQoL M = 12.11) and mild symptoms of depression and anxiety (PHQ-9 M = 9.92; GAD-7 M = 9.26).
More information can be found in Appendix A.

There were no significant differences in baseline characteristics (including age, gender, nationality, education level, marital status, current professional help and clinical scores) between the two intervention arms (all p > .05).

>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Discussion</head>

text.text: This randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing two intervention conditions showed no significant difference in adherence for the total sample (1.85 of 4 modules in the gamified and 1.7 of 4 in the non-gamified intervention).

However, when analyzing intervention starters (i.e. participants who completed at least one module and were therefore exposed to the gamification elements), the gamified version was associated with a small but statistically significant increase in modules completed compared to the non-gamified version (2.86 and 2.64 modules respectively, Cohen's d = .17).
No significant differences were found between the gamified and non-gamified intervention in satisfaction, satisfaction with e-coach guidance, or clinical outcomes.

Participants in both groups reported moderate to high satisfaction, and showed significant improvements in self-esteem, depressive symptoms, anxiety, and quality of life, with moderate to large effect sizes (Cohen's d = .44-.76).

These findings suggest that gamification may have a small effect on adherence within intervention starters, though this does not appear to translate into higher satisfaction or improved clinical outcomes.

Overall, both versions of the intervention were associated with meaningful improvements over time, suggesting that the core intervention, rather than the gamification elements, may be the primary driver of change.
Our findings are in line with prior literature suggesting that gamification can enhance engagement and participation in digital interventions (Looyestyn et al., 2017; Seaborn & Fels, 2015).
text.formatted: Our findings are in line with prior literature suggesting that gamification can enhance engagement and participation in digital interventions <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Looyestyn et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Seaborn & Fels, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, meta-analytic evidence indicates that gamification tends to produce small to moderate improvements in engagement-related outcomes (C. Cheng & Ebrahimi, 2023), which was replicated in our study amongst intervention starters.
text.formatted: Indeed, meta-analytic evidence indicates that gamification tends to produce small to moderate improvements in engagement-related outcomes (C. <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Cheng & Ebrahimi, 2023)</ref>, which was replicated in our study amongst intervention starters.

text.text: However, contrary to our expectations, gamification had no significant effect on the satisfaction or clinical outcomes in this study.
There are several possible explanations for this absence.
The impact of gamification may depend on the type and quality of game elements (Hamari et al., 2014; Sailer et al., 2017).
text.formatted: The impact of gamification may depend on the type and quality of game elements <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Hamari et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Sailer et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: It is possible that the gamification elements in EsteemUp (i.e. progress bar, badges, unlockable content, and a certificate of completion) were not engaging or relevant enough for the students.
Alternatively, the high baseline quality of the intervention and platform may have resulted in a ceiling effect.
Given the relatively high satisfaction scores observed in both conditions, there may have been limited room for gamification to significantly improve engagement, satisfaction, or clinical outcomes.
Adherence in the total sample was on the lower side when compared to other digital mental health interventions for students (Harrer et al., 2018; Palacios et al., 2018; Rith-Najarian et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Adherence in the total sample was on the lower side when compared to other digital mental health interventions for students <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Harrer et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Palacios et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">Rith-Najarian et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This may be attributable to the real-world context of our study, which did not include financial incentives, as well as the relatively low level of mental health complaints in our sample.
However, among intervention starters, nearly half completed it.
This relatively high completion rate for a real-world intervention may indicate good acceptability among students and reflect a challenge in uptake rather than in adherence.
Regarding clinical outcomes, we found moderate to large improvements on all measures across intervention arms.

Previous research on digital mental health interventions for students generally demonstrated small to moderate improvements in outcomes such as self-esteem, depression and anxiety (Bruhns et al., 2021; Clore & Gaynor, 2006; Cuijpers, Miguel, et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Previous research on digital mental health interventions for students generally demonstrated small to moderate improvements in outcomes such as self-esteem, depression and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Bruhns et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Clore & Gaynor, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Cuijpers, Miguel, et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, we found two large effect sizes (on self-esteem and quality of life), which exceeded the small-to-moderate effects typically reported in previous research.

Though the absence of an inactive control group prevents us from definitively attributing these changes to the intervention, our findings provide preliminary support for the intervention's potential to improve selfesteem and several related mental health outcomes.
Interestingly, intervention adherence was not associated with clinical outcomes in the present study.

This is consistent with two previous studies on digital self-esteem interventions for students, which also found no relationship between adherence and clinical outcomes (Berg et al., 2022; Bruhns et al., 2021).
text.formatted: This is consistent with two previous studies on digital self-esteem interventions for students, which also found no relationship between adherence and clinical outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Berg et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Bruhns et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: This contrasts with evidence suggesting that higher adherence is generally linked to better treatment outcomes (Donkin et al., 2011; Linardon, 2026; Linardon & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, 2020).
text.formatted: This contrasts with evidence suggesting that higher adherence is generally linked to better treatment outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Donkin et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Linardon, 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">Linardon & Fuller-Tyszkiewicz, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One possible explanation is self-selection bias, which refers to systematic differences in those who choose to continue or discontinue an intervention.

Indeed, attrition in digital interventions typically follows one of two patterns: participants may drop out due to lack of engagement or motivation, or they may drop out due to early improvement (Eysenbach, 2005).
text.formatted: Indeed, attrition in digital interventions typically follows one of two patterns: participants may drop out due to lack of engagement or motivation, or they may drop out due to early improvement <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Eysenbach, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: These opposing patterns may cancel each other out statistically, thereby weakening or obscuring conclusions that can be drawn on the relationship between adherence and treatment outcomes.
Another possible explanation is that a higher intervention dose may not necessarily result in greater clinical improvement.
This interpretation is consistent with literature demonstrating that meaningful improvements can occur after a single, well-designed therapeutic session (Schleider et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This interpretation is consistent with literature demonstrating that meaningful improvements can occur after a single, well-designed therapeutic session <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">(Schleider et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The findings of the present study should be interpreted considering several limitations.

Firstly, our study did not include process measures to understand and assess the mechanisms behind gamification, such as intrinsic motivation or user curiosity or interest (V. W. S. Cheng et al., 2019; Ryan et al., 2006; Seaborn & Fels, 2015).
text.formatted: Firstly, our study did not include process measures to understand and assess the mechanisms behind gamification, such as intrinsic motivation or user curiosity or interest (V. W. S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Cheng et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">Ryan et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Seaborn & Fels, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: Including such measures would have allowed us to examine not only whether gamification had an impact, but also how and why in this specific context.
As a result, the current study cannot provide insight into the mechanisms that underlie effective or ineffective gamification.
Another limitation is the absence of an inactive control group (e.g. waitlist).

Although participants showed improvements in self-esteem, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life, these changes may also be due to alternative factors such as natural symptom fluctuation, regression to the mean, or external influences unrelated to the intervention (Barnett et al., 2005).
text.formatted: Although participants showed improvements in self-esteem, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and quality of life, these changes may also be due to alternative factors such as natural symptom fluctuation, regression to the mean, or external influences unrelated to the intervention <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Barnett et al., 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Consequently, the observed improvements should be interpreted cautiously, and causal conclusions regarding intervention effectiveness cannot be drawn.

Lastly, our final sample was substantially smaller than required based on the a priori power calculation because of considerable attrition, resulting in lower statistical power than originally intended.
In addition, the observed effect size was smaller than anticipated, meaning that a considerably larger sample would have been required to detect such effects.
Consequently, the combination of the reduced sample size and smaller-than-expected effects likely limited our ability to detect statistically significant between-group differences.
The present study also demonstrates several strengths.
First, it contributes to the growing body of literature on gamification in digital mental health.
To our knowledge, no study has isolated the specific effect of gamification on adherence and effectiveness by directly comparing two versions of an otherwise identical intervention.
Most RCTs on gamified digital mental health interventions compared a gamified intervention to an inactive control or waitlist (Aschentrup et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Most RCTs on gamified digital mental health interventions compared a gamified intervention to an inactive control or waitlist <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Aschentrup et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: There has been a call for "research that isolates the impacts of gamification to determine its effectiveness in the health and wellbeing domain" (Johnson et al., 2016), which is a gap addressed by the present study.
text.formatted: There has been a call for "research that isolates the impacts of gamification to determine its effectiveness in the health and wellbeing domain" <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Johnson et al., 2016)</ref>, which is a gap addressed by the present study.

text.text: A final strength of this study is its real-world setting.

EsteemUp was embedded into the service offering of several universities, which allowed us to examine how students engage with the intervention under natural conditions, as opposed to controlled research environments.
As such, the present findings may offer valuable insight into the implementation of gamified mental health interventions in real-world higher education settings.
A recommendation for future research pertains to the selection and evaluation of the gamification elements.
As Cheng et al. (2019) stated in their systematic review: "researchers may treat gamification as a black box without consideration for its underlying mechanisms" (V. W. S. Cheng et al., 2019).
text.formatted: As <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Cheng et al. (2019)</ref> stated in their systematic review: "researchers may treat gamification as a black box without consideration for its underlying mechanisms" (V. W. S. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">Cheng et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should therefore ensure that gamification features are appropriately tailored to the target population, ideally through early involvement of end users in the design and selection process.
Due to time constraints, this form of preliminary user input was not feasible in the present study, although it may have improved the relevance and acceptability of the gamification elements.
In addition, future research should include process measures such as motivation, interest, and engagement with the gamification elements.
Together, these approaches would strengthen understanding of why, how, and under what conditions gamification contributes to intervention effectiveness.
Additionally, a natural continuation of this study would be to conduct a randomized controlled trial (RCT) to assess the clinical effectiveness of EsteemUp.

We compared two active treatments in the present study, and though we did see improvements from pre-to post-test in self-esteem, depression, anxiety and quality of life, these cannot be directly attributed to the intervention.
Therefore, future research should conduct an RCT that includes a waitlist or inactive control condition to more thoroughly assess the effectiveness of EsteemUp.

The addition of gamification elements to a digital self-esteem intervention produced a small significant increase in adherence amongst intervention starters but did not enhance satisfaction or clinical outcomes.

Improvements in self-esteem, depression, anxiety, and quality of life were observed in both the gamified and non-gamified version of the intervention, highlighting the potential of digital self-esteem interventions to support students' mental health.
Future research should explore which gamification elements best fit the preferences of the target demographic, as well as assess the psychological mechanisms that underlie gamification.
Additionally, a randomized controlled trial using an inactive control would allow for firmer conclusions regarding intervention effectiveness.
